memoryText: And I will betroth you to me forever. I will betroth you to me in righteousness and in justice, in steadfast love and in mercy.
readingInstruction: No new reading today. Read Hosea 2:19 slowly, several times, and then say it from memory. Read the meditation and the week in review, and choose one of the three questions to write about, pray over, or share with someone.
memoryVerseMeditation:
This promise is spoken to an unfaithful wife. It is the Bible’s most tender picture of what God intends for his people.

“And I will betroth you to me forever.” To betroth is to make a solemn promise of marriage. It is the beginning of a covenant. Israel had broken the covenant again and again, but God does not take back his love. The word “forever” stands out. This is not a temporary arrangement that could be broken again. It is a permanent commitment.

The word “betroth” is repeated three times in verses 19 and 20, as if God cannot say it enough. A man who had been wronged has every reason to refuse. Yet he says it again and again.

“In righteousness and in justice.” These are the foundation of the new marriage. This is not sentimental love that ignores wrong. It is a love that is built on what is right. In the new covenant, justice is satisfied, not set aside. The cross is where righteousness and love meet.

“In steadfast love and in mercy.” These are the heart of the covenant. Steadfast love is covenant loyalty, the faithful love that does not let go. Mercy is compassion toward the needy. God promises to give them to his people, not because of their record but because of who he is.

The verse that follows adds, “And you shall know the LORD.” The goal of the marriage is a relationship of knowledge. The people will know their husband.

For the Christian, this promise is realized in Christ. He is the bridegroom, and the church is his bride. He has paid the price. “I will betroth you to me forever” is a promise for you, if you are in him. Say it as a statement of what God has done.
weekInReview: This week you read the psalms of injustice: Psalms 58, 82, 94, 109, 140, and 142, the cries of those who suffer under corrupt power, with the confidence that there is a God who judges on earth. You saw that Jesus quoted Psalm 82 and that God stands at the right hand of the needy. And you began the book of Hosea, the prophet whose marriage to an unfaithful woman became a picture of God’s love for Israel. You read about the children with names like No Mercy and Not My People, and about the God who allures his wayward bride into the wilderness and speaks tenderly to her. You saw Hosea buy back Gomer, and you heard the promise: I will betroth you to me forever. The week taught that God hears the cry of the oppressed, and that his love is stronger than his people’s unfaithfulness.
reflectionQuestions: The psalms of this week take honest, angry prayers to God. What injustice or hurt do you need to bring to him in prayer rather than in action?
Hosea buys back his unfaithful wife, a picture of Christ redeeming his people. What does it mean to you that you were bought at a price?
God says he will “speak tenderly” to Israel in the wilderness. Where do you need to hear his tenderness right now?
prayerPrompts: Thank God for betrothing you to himself forever.
Thank him for buying you back at the cost of his Son.
Ask him to speak tenderly to you this Sabbath.
